Document Title: StickyMemory: Robust Web Agents with Episodic Memory and Self-Verification
Author Affiliations: Raymond James & Associates / Independent Researcher, St. Petersburg, FL, USA
Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, and AI Applications (ICCSDFAI)
Abstract: Tools effects are never checked, and early decisions are often lost, which makes web agents very difficult with long and multi-step tasks. We introduce StickyMemory, a simple controller that combines a behavior-cloned actuator with two extensions rolling episodic memory summaries and a simple self-verifier that reflows key steps to establish DOM and tool invariants. In case of a mismatch being recognized a plan-repair phase also restarts where the last consistent checkpoint was rather than starting the episode from the beginning. StickyMemory is tested on WebArena, VisualWebArena and Mind2Web, benchmarked against ReAct, Reflexion, and no-memory policy on standardized prompts, tools, seeds, and step-budgets. StickyMemory increases success rates, decreases timeouts and steps across test suites, e.g., in WebArena, it increases success to 64.6% and in VisualWebArena, it increases success to 58.9% and in Mind2Web, it increases success to 59.1%, and the median steps is lower, and the timeouts are also lower than strong prompts baselines. The verifier is highly precise and recalls, and ablations exhibit a distinct knee in its performance at a small memory horizon. It has a modular design that makes it model-agnostic and can be retrofitted to existing web agents.

Abstract: Significant efforts have been dedicated to employing model-checking as a formal verification approach in the context of smart contracts. Abstract: Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) play an essential role in industrial automation by managing complex safety-critical processes. Abstract: Mobile apps have been an integral part in our daily life. While existing work has provided both static and dynamic analysis to build the WTG for an app, the constructed WTG misses many transitions or contains many infeasible transitions due to the coverage issues of dynamic analysis and over-approximation of the static analysis. We propose ProMal, a "tribrid" analysis that synergistically combines static analysis, dynamic analysis, and machine learning to construct a precise WTG. For the unverified transitions, ProMal further provides machine learning techniques that leverage runtime information (i.e., screenshots, UI layouts, and text information) to predict whether they are feasible transitions. Manual translation into formal languages such as SMT-LIB is slow and error-prone. We present VeriODD, a tool that automates this translation. The tool integrates with SMT solvers such as Z3 to provide automated consistency checks of ODD specifications and verification of COD conformance. A graphical user interface supports editing specifications, inspecting generated formulas, and performing verification with a single click. VeriODD thereby closes the gap between stakeholder-friendly ODD/COD notations and formal verification, enabling scalable and automated assurance of operational boundaries in autonomous driving.

Abstract: This paper presents SAFEST, a powerful tool for modelling and analyzing both static and dynamic fault trees. The backbone of the analysis is based on efficient state space generation. SAFEST is state of the art for DFT analysis, as demonstrated by an experimental evaluation and comparison with existing tools. Document Title: Improving Automated GUI Testing by Learning to Avoid Infeasible Tests
Author Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, The University of Sheffield, UK
Publication Title: 2020 IEEE International Conference On Artificial Intelligence Testing (AITest)
Abstract: Most modern end-user software applications are controlled through a graphical user interface (GUI). When it comes to automated test selection, however, GUIs present two major challenges: (1) It is difficult to automatically identify feasible, non-trivial sequences of GUI interactions (test cases), and (2) each attempt at a test case execution can take a long time, eliminating the possibility of rapidly attempting large numbers of alternatives. In this paper we present an iterative approach that infers state-machine models from previous test executions, and increases the utility of tests by learning which sequences to avoid. The approach is evaluated on a selection of Java applications, and the results indicate that our approach is successful at achieving higher code coverage and longer sequences than the state of the art, albeit with a time-overhead caused by the repeated invocation of a Machine Learner.
